cases.question: What did Apple disclose in its fiscal 2024 10-K about the European Commission's Digital Markets Act investigations, and what could the Commission do if it finds a violation?
cases.expected_text: On March 25, 2024 the Commission opened two formal noncompliance investigations under the DMA: one under Article 5(4) on how developers may communicate and promote offers to users of App Store apps and conclude contracts with them, and one under Article 6(3) on default settings, uninstalling apps and a browser choice screen on iOS. On June 24, 2024 it issued preliminary findings that Apple's App Store rules breach the DMA and opened a third investigation into Apple's new contractual requirements for third-party developers and app marketplaces. If the Commission finds a violation it can issue a cease and desist order and impose fines of up to 10% of Apple's annual worldwide net sales, and its order would apply immediately during an appeal unless stayed. Apple says it believes it complies with the DMA.
key_points: Two formal noncompliance investigations were opened in March 2024: Article 5(4) (how developers communicate and promote offers and conclude contracts) and Article 6(3) (defaults, uninstallation and browser choice).
Preliminary findings in June 2024 said the App Store rules breach the DMA, and a third investigation into new contractual requirements was opened.
A violation can bring a cease and desist order and fines of up to 10% of annual worldwide net sales.
Apple believes it complies with the DMA.

passages.quote: On March 25, 2024, the Commission announced that it had opened two formal noncompliance investigations against the Company under the DMA.

The Commission’s investigations concern (1) Article 5(4) of the DMA, which relates to how developers may communicate and promote offers to end users for apps distributed through the App Store as well as how developers may conclude contracts with those end users; and (2) Article 6(3) of the DMA, which relates to default settings, uninstallation of apps, and a web browser choice screen on iOS.

On June 24, 2024, the Commission announced its preliminary findings in the Article 5(4) investigation alleging that the Company’s App Store rules are in breach of the DMA and announced that it had opened a third formal investigation against the Company regarding whether the Company’s new contractual requirements for third-party app developers and app marketplaces may violate the DMA.
If the Commission makes a final determination that there has been a violation, it can issue a cease and desist order and may impose fines up to 10% of the Company’s annual worldwide net sales.

Although any decision by the Commission can be appealed to the General Court of the EU, the effectiveness of the Commission’s order would apply immediately while the appeal is pending, unless a stay of the order is granted.
The Company believes that it complies with the DMA and has continued to make changes to its compliance plan in response to feedback and engagement with the Commission.

cases.question: How does Apple describe the risks of its dependence on outsourcing partners and single-source suppliers in its fiscal 2024 10-K?
cases.expected_text: Apple says substantially all of its manufacturing is performed in whole or in part by outsourcing partners located primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam, with a significant concentration at a small number of partners, often in single locations. While these arrangements can lower operating costs, they reduce Apple's direct control over production and distribution. Because it obtains certain components from single or limited sources, Apple is subject to significant supply and pricing risks.
key_points: Substantially all manufacturing is done by outsourcing partners concentrated in a few Asian countries and a small number of partners, often in single locations.
Outsourcing reduces Apple's direct control over production and distribution.
Single- or limited-source components expose Apple to significant supply and pricing risks.

passages.quote: Substantially all of the Company’s manufacturing is performed in whole or in part by outsourcing partners located primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam, and a significant concentration of this manufacturing is currently performed by a small number of outsourcing partners, often in single locations.
While these arrangements can lower operating costs, they also reduce the Company’s direct control over production and distribution.
Because the Company currently obtains certain components from single or limited sources, the Company is subject to significant supply and pricing risks.

cases.question: Describe the preterm infant formula (NEC) litigation Abbott disclosed in its 2023 10-K.
cases.expected_text: Abbott is a party to lawsuits alleging that preterm infants developed necrotizing enterocolitis after being given a cow's milk-based preterm infant formula product, resulting in personal injuries or death. As of January 31, 2024 there were 993 such lawsuits pending in federal and state courts in which Abbott is a party; plaintiffs seek various damages, including punitive damages. In April 2022 the federal cases were consolidated for pretrial purposes in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois.
key_points: The suits allege preterm infants developed necrotizing enterocolitis from a cow's milk-based preterm infant formula.
993 lawsuits were pending as of January 31, 2024, seeking damages including punitive damages.
Federal cases were consolidated for pretrial purposes in the Northern District of Illinois.

passages.quote: The lawsuits allege that preterm infants developed necrotizing enterocolitis as a result of being administered a cow’s milk-based preterm infant formula product, which resulted in personal injuries or death. As of January 31, 2024, there were 993 lawsuits pending in federal and state courts in which Abbott is a party. The plaintiffs seek various damages, including punitive damages.
In April 2022, the U.S. Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation ordered all federal court cases consolidated for pretrial purposes in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois.

cases.question: What happened to Adobe's proposed acquisition of Figma according to its fiscal 2023 10-K?
cases.expected_text: Adobe agreed on September 15, 2022 to acquire Figma for about $20 billion, roughly half cash and half stock. On December 17, 2023 the two companies entered into a mutual termination agreement ending the merger, and on December 20, 2023 Adobe paid Figma a $1 billion termination fee from cash on hand.
key_points: The deal, signed in September 2022, valued Figma at about $20 billion, half cash and half stock.
The merger was terminated by mutual agreement in December 2023.
Adobe paid Figma a $1 billion termination fee using cash on hand.

passages.quote: On September 15, 2022, we entered into a definitive merger agreement under which we intended to acquire Figma, Inc. (“Figma”) for approximately $20 billion, comprised of approximately half cash and half stock. On December 17, 2023, we entered into a mutual termination agreement with Figma to terminate the proposed merger. In accordance with the terms of the termination agreement, on December 20, 2023, we paid Figma a termination fee of $1 billion using cash on hand.

cases.question: How did AMD's segments contribute to the change in its 2023 net revenue?
cases.expected_text: AMD's 2023 net revenue fell 4%. Client segment revenue fell 25% on lower processor sales and Gaming fell 9% on lower semi-custom sales. These were partly offset by a 17% rise in Embedded revenue, reflecting a full year of Xilinx versus a partial period in 2022, and a 7% rise in Data Center revenue on higher sales of AMD Instinct GPUs and 4th Gen EPYC CPUs.
key_points: Client revenue fell on lower processor sales and Gaming fell on lower semi-custom sales.
Embedded revenue rose because Xilinx was included for the full year.
Data Center revenue rose on Instinct GPU and 4th Gen EPYC CPU sales.

passages.quote: Against the backdrop of a mixed demand environment, net revenue for 2023 was $22.7 billion, a decrease of 4% compared to 2022 net revenue of $23.6 billion.

The decrease in net revenue was primarily due to a 25% decrease in Client segment revenue primarily due to lower processor sales and a 9% decrease in Gaming segment revenue primarily due to lower semi-custom product sales. This decrease was partially offset by a 17% increase in Embedded segment revenue primarily due to the inclusion of embedded product revenue from Xilinx, Inc. (Xilinx) for the full twelve months period in 2023, as compared to a partial period from February 14, 2022 (the Xilinx Acquisition Date) in the prior year period, and a 7% increase in Data Center segment revenue primarily driven by higher sales of AMD Instinct GPUs and 4th Gen AMD EPYC CPUs.

cases.question: Why did Amazon report a large other expense in 2022, and how does it account for its Rivian investment?
cases.expected_text: Other income (expense), net swung from $14.6 billion of income in 2021 to $(16.8) billion in 2022, driven largely by a $(12.7) billion valuation loss on Amazon's equity investment in Rivian (after an $11.8 billion gain in 2021). Amazon held about 17% of Rivian's Class A stock, judged it had significant influence (through the investment, its EV purchase arrangement and a board seat), and elected the fair value option, carrying the stake in marketable securities so price changes flow through other income (expense).
key_points: The 2022 other expense was driven mainly by a $12.7 billion valuation loss on the Rivian investment.
Amazon has significant influence over Rivian (about 17% ownership) but elected the fair value option.
Rivian fair value changes are recorded in other income (expense), net.

passages.quote: Other income (expense), net was $14.6 billion and $(16.8) billion during 2021 and 2022. The primary components of other income (expense), net are related to equity securities valuations and adjustments, equity warrant valuations, and foreign currency. Included in other income (expense), net in 2021 and 2022 is a marketable equity securities valuation gain (loss) of $11.8 billion and $(12.7) billion from our equity investment in Rivian.
As of December 31, 2022, we held 158 million shares of Rivian’s Class A common stock, representing an approximate 17% ownership interest, and an approximate 16% voting interest.

We determined that we have the ability to exercise significant influence over Rivian through our equity investment, our commercial arrangement for the purchase of electric vehicles, and one of our employees serving on Rivian’s board of directors. We elected the fair value option to account for our equity investment in Rivian, which is included in “Marketable securities” on our consolidated balance sheets.

cases.question: How did Broadcom acquire VMware and what is its strategy for the VMware business, per its fiscal 2024 10-K?
cases.expected_text: Broadcom completed the VMware merger on November 22, 2023 in a cash-and-stock deal: about $30.8 billion in cash and 544 million Broadcom shares worth $53.4 billion, with the cash funded by $30.4 billion of term loans and cash on hand. It then sold VMware's end-user computing business to KKR for $3.5 billion. Its strategy is to focus on VMware's core business of private cloud environments on-premises for large enterprises, divest non-core assets, simplify the product portfolio and move from perpetual to subscription licensing; it warns that if customers do not accept this strategy it could lose significant customers.
key_points: The VMware merger closed November 22, 2023 for about $30.8 billion cash plus 544 million shares (fair value $53.4 billion).
The end-user computing business was sold to KKR for $3.5 billion.
Strategy: focus on core private cloud for large enterprises and divest non-core assets.
Shift from perpetual to subscription licensing, with a risk that customers reject it.

passages.quote: On November 22, 2023, we acquired VMware in a cash-and-stock transaction (the “VMware Merger”), in which VMware stockholders received, in aggregate, approximately $30.8 billion in cash and 544 million shares of Broadcom common stock (on a split adjusted basis) with a fair value of $53.4 billion.

We funded the cash portion of the VMware Merger consideration with net proceeds from the issuance of $30.4 billion in term loans under a credit agreement that we entered into on August 15, 2023, as well as cash on hand.
Following the VMware Merger, we sold VMware’s end-user computing business to KKR & Co. Inc. for cash consideration of $3.5 billion, after working capital adjustments.

As part of our integration of the VMware business, we are focusing on VMware’s core business of creating private cloud environments on-premises among large enterprises globally and divesting non-core assets. If VMware customers do not accept our business strategy, including our transition from a perpetual to a subscription licensing model and our simplified product portfolio, the investments we have made or may make to implement our strategy may be of no or limited value, we may lose significant customers, our financial results may be adversely affected and our stock price may suffer.

cases.question: How does Constellation describe the IRA nuclear production tax credit and its expected effect on its nuclear fleet (2023 10-K)?
cases.expected_text: The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 created a nuclear production tax credit of up to $15 per MWh, subject to phase-out, from 2024 through 2032, adjusted annually for inflation. Starting in 2024 Constellation's nuclear fleet is eligible for units not already receiving state support. The credit provides increasing support as unit revenues fall below IRA thresholds, making it an important tool for managing commodity price risk. With this support, Constellation expects its nuclear assets to operate through the end of the credit period.
key_points: The nuclear PTC is up to $15/MWh, subject to phase-out, for 2024-2032, adjusted for inflation.
Support rises as unit revenues fall below IRA levels, which helps manage commodity price risk.
Constellation expects its nuclear assets to operate through the end of the PTC period.

passages.quote: Beginning in 2024, our nuclear fleet is eligible for the nuclear PTC provided by the IRA, an important tool in managing commodity price risk for each nuclear unit not already receiving state support. The nuclear PTC provides increasing levels of support as unit revenues decline below levels established in the IRA and is further adjusted annually for inflation over the duration of the program.

The nuclear PTC recognizes the contributions of carbon-free nuclear power by providing a federal tax credit of up to $15 per MWh, subject to phase-out, beginning in 2024 and continuing through 2032. The nuclear PTC includes annual adjustments for inflation. With the nuclear PTC policy support, we expect our nuclear assets will operate through the end of the nuclear PTC period.

cases.question: How does Costco value its merchandise inventories, according to its fiscal 2024 10-K?
cases.expected_text: U.S. merchandise inventories are valued by the cost method on a LIFO basis, which Costco believes more fairly presents results by more closely matching current costs with current revenues. It records an adjustment each quarter, if necessary, for the projected annual effect of inflation or deflation, and adjusts these estimates to actual results at year-end. An immaterial LIFO benefit was recorded in 2024, after an immaterial charge in 2023. Canadian and Other International merchandise inventories are valued mainly with the cost and retail inventory methods, respectively, on a FIFO basis.
key_points: U.S. inventories are valued on a LIFO basis.
Quarterly LIFO adjustments for projected inflation or deflation are trued up at year-end; 2024 had an immaterial LIFO benefit.
Canadian and Other International inventories use FIFO.

passages.quote: U.S. merchandise inventories are valued by the cost method of accounting, using the last-in, first-out (LIFO) basis. The Company believes the LIFO method more fairly presents the results of operations by more closely matching current costs with current revenues.

The Company records an adjustment each quarter, if necessary, for the projected annual effect of inflation or deflation, and these estimates are adjusted to actual results determined at year-end, after actual inflation or deflation rates and inventory levels have been determined.
An immaterial LIFO benefit was recorded in 2024 and an immaterial charge was recorded in 2023.
Canadian and Other International merchandise inventories are predominantly valued using the cost and retail inventory methods, respectively, using the first-in, first-out (FIFO) basis.

cases.question: What changes did Costco make to its membership fees in fiscal 2024, and how did membership revenue and renewal rates develop?
cases.expected_text: Effective September 1, 2024, Costco raised U.S. and Canada Gold Star, Business and Business affiliate fees to $65 a year and the Executive fee from $120 to $130, and raised the maximum annual 2% Executive reward from $1,000 to $1,250. Membership fee revenue grew 5% in 2024, driven by new sign-ups and Executive upgrades, partly offset by one less week of fee income. Year-end renewal rates were 92.9% in the U.S. and Canada and 90.5% worldwide.
key_points: Fees rose effective September 1, 2024 (to $65 basic and $130 Executive) and the maximum Executive reward rose to $1,250.
Membership fee revenue rose 5% on sign-ups and Executive upgrades, partly offset by one less week.
Renewal rates were 92.9% in the U.S. and Canada and 90.5% worldwide.

passages.quote: Effective September 1, 2024, we increased our membership fees in the U.S. and Canada for Gold Star, Business, and Business affiliates to $65 per year. The Executive membership fee increased from $120 to $130 (membership fee of $65, plus Executive upgrade of $65), and the maximum annual 2% reward associated with the Executive Membership increased from $1,000 to $1,250.

Membership fee revenue increased 5% in 2024, driven by new member sign-ups and upgrades to Executive Membership. These increases were partially offset by one less week of membership fee income in 2024. At the end of 2024, our member renewal rates were 92.9% in the U.S. and Canada and 90.5% worldwide.

cases.question: What capital return and cost actions did Salesforce describe in its fiscal 2024 10-K?
cases.expected_text: Salesforce had never declared a cash dividend before February 2024; on February 28, 2024 it announced a quarterly dividend policy and its first-ever cash dividend of $0.40 per share, payable April 11, 2024. During fiscal 2024 it repurchased about 36 million shares of its common stock for about $7.7 billion. On costs, its Restructuring Plan announced in January 2023 was intended to reduce operating costs and improve operating margins through a workforce reduction (substantially completed by the end of fiscal 2024) and select real estate exits and office space reductions expected to be completed by the end of fiscal 2026.
key_points: Salesforce announced its first-ever quarterly cash dividend ($0.40 per share) in February 2024.
It repurchased about $7.7 billion of its shares in fiscal 2024.
The January 2023 Restructuring Plan cut the workforce and real estate to reduce costs and improve operating margins.

passages.quote: Share Repurchase Program: During the fiscal year ended January 31, 2024, we repurchased approximately 36 million shares of our common stock for approximately $7.7 billion.

Prior to February 2024, we had never declared or paid any cash dividends on our common stock. On February 28, 2024, we announced a quarterly dividend policy and the declaration of our first-ever cash dividend. This cash dividend of $0.40 per share of the Company’s outstanding common stock will be paid on April 11, 2024 to stockholders of record as of the close of business on March 14, 2024.

In January 2023, we announced the Restructuring Plan, which was intended to reduce operating costs, improve operating margins and continue advancing our ongoing commitment to profitable growth. The Restructuring Plan included a reduction of our workforce, which was substantially completed by the end of fiscal 2024, and select real estate exits and office space reductions within certain markets, which are expected to be completed by the end of fiscal 2026.

cases.question: What does Alphabet's 2023 10-K say about the U.S. Department of Justice antitrust case concerning Search?
cases.expected_text: Alphabet began receiving civil investigative demands from the DOJ in August 2019, requesting information about its prior antitrust investigations and certain aspects of its business. On October 20, 2020 the DOJ and a number of state Attorneys General sued in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, alleging Google violated U.S. antitrust laws relating to Search and Search advertising. The trial ended on November 16, 2023 and Alphabet expected a decision in 2024.
key_points: The DOJ began sending civil investigative demands in August 2019.
The DOJ and state Attorneys General sued in October 2020 alleging antitrust violations in Search and Search advertising.
The trial ended on November 16, 2023, with a decision expected in 2024.

passages.quote: In August 2019, we began receiving civil investigative demands from the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) requesting information and documents relating to our prior antitrust investigations and certain aspects of our business.

The DOJ and a number of state Attorneys General filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia on October 20, 2020 alleging that Google violated U.S. antitrust laws relating to Search and Search advertising. The trial ended on November 16, 2023, and we expect a decision in 2024.

cases.question: What is Intel's 2024 Restructuring Plan and what does it involve?
cases.expected_text: In 2024 Intel announced a series of cost and capital reduction initiatives, called the 2024 Restructuring Plan, designed to adjust its spending to current business trends while enabling its new operating model and continuing to fund its core strategy of returning to product and process competitiveness. It includes cutting headcount (about a 15% reduction in the core Intel workforce by early 2025), consolidating and shrinking its real estate footprint, 'clean sheet' portfolio reviews, rationalizing capital investments by demand and capacity needs, and reducing operating expenses. Intel recognized $2.8 billion of restructuring charges in 2024.
key_points: The plan aims to cut costs and capital spending while funding a return to product and process competitiveness.
It includes about a 15% reduction in the core workforce by early 2025, real estate consolidation, portfolio reviews and capex rationalization.
Intel recognized $2.8 billion of restructuring charges in 2024.

passages.quote: In 2024, we announced our intention to implement a series of cost and capital reduction initiatives designed to adjust our spending to current business trends while enabling our new operating model and continuing to fund investments in our core strategy—returning to product and process competitiveness.

These initiatives, which we refer to as our 2024 Restructuring Plan, include reducing headcount, consolidating and reducing our global real estate footprint, conducting portfolio reviews of our businesses under a "clean sheet" view, rationalizing capital investments and deployments based upon demand signals and capacity requirements, and reducing our overall operating expenses. The headcount actions in connection with the 2024 Restructuring Plan are expected to result in an approximate 15% decrease in our core Intel workforce by early 2025. As a result of initiating and deploying our 2024 Restructuring Plan, we recognized restructuring charges of $2.8 billion in 2024.

cases.question: Why did Intel record a valuation allowance against its U.S. deferred tax assets in 2024?
cases.expected_text: Intel assesses the recoverability of its deferred tax assets quarterly, weighing positive and negative evidence. In the third quarter of 2024 it concluded it was more likely than not that its U.S. federal deferred tax assets would not be recovered, because of its three-year cumulative historical loss position, which resulted largely from the asset impairment, restructuring and other charges taken in that quarter. The resulting valuation allowance drove a higher 2024 effective tax rate and about $9.9 billion of non-cash charges to the tax provision.
key_points: Intel concluded in Q3 2024 that its U.S. federal deferred tax assets were more likely than not unrecoverable.
The trigger was a three-year cumulative loss position, driven largely by Q3 2024 impairment and restructuring charges.
The allowance raised the 2024 effective tax rate (about $9.9 billion of non-cash tax charges).

passages.quote: Our effective tax rate increased in 2024 compared to 2023, primarily driven by the effects associated with the establishment of a valuation allowance against our US federal deferred tax assets in 2024. We assess the recoverability of our deferred tax assets quarterly, weighing available positive and negative evidence. As a result of our assessment in the third quarter of 2024, we determined it was more likely than not that the deferred tax assets will not be recoverable based upon our three-year cumulative historical loss position as of the third quarter of 2024, largely resulting from the asset impairment and restructuring and other charges incurred during the third quarter of 2024.
$9.9 billion of non-cash charges recorded to provision for income taxes that substantially related to valuation allowances recorded to our net deferred tax assets

cases.question: Summarize Coca-Cola's dispute with the IRS over transfer pricing as described in its 2023 10-K, including where the litigation stands and how the company has reserved for it.
cases.expected_text: In September 2015 the IRS issued a Notice of Deficiency seeking about $3.3 billion of additional federal income tax for 2007-2009, stating its intent to reallocate over $9 billion of income to the U.S. parent company from foreign affiliates it licensed to make and sell its products outside the U.S. The Tax Court's November 2020 opinion predominantly sided with the IRS, while agreeing that dividends previously paid by the foreign licensees could continue to offset royalties, and a November 2023 supplemental opinion also sided with the IRS on the blocked-income regulations. Coca-Cola's conclusion that it is more likely than not its tax positions will ultimately be sustained on appeal is unchanged, and it updated its tax reserve to $439 million as of December 31, 2023.
key_points: The IRS sought about $3.3 billion of additional tax for 2007-2009, reallocating over $9 billion of income to the U.S. parent from licensed foreign affiliates.
The Tax Court's 2020 opinion predominantly sided with the IRS.
A November 2023 supplemental opinion also sided with the IRS (blocked-income regulations).
The company believes it is more likely than not that its tax positions will ultimately be sustained on appeal.
The tax reserve was updated to $439 million as of December 31, 2023.

passages.quote: On September 17, 2015, the Company received a Statutory Notice of Deficiency (“Notice”) from the IRS seeking approximately $3.3 billion of additional federal income tax for years 2007 through 2009.

In the Notice, the IRS stated its intent to reallocate over $9 billion of income to the U.S. parent company from certain of its foreign affiliates that the U.S. parent company licensed to manufacture, distribute, sell, market and promote its products in certain non-U.S. markets.

On November 18, 2020, the Tax Court issued the Opinion in which it predominantly sided with the IRS but agreed with the Company that dividends previously paid by the foreign licensees to the U.S. parent company in reliance upon the Closing Agreement should continue to be allowed to offset royalties, including those that would become payable to the Company in accordance with the Opinion.

On November 8, 2023, the Tax Court issued a supplemental opinion, siding with the IRS in concluding both that the blocked-income regulations apply to the Company’s operations and that the Tax Court opinion in 3M Co. & Subs. v. Commissioner (February 9, 2023) controlled as to the validity of those regulations.
The Company’s conclusion that it is more likely than not the Company’s tax positions will ultimately be sustained on appeal is unchanged as of December 31, 2023.
we updated our tax reserve as of December 31, 2023 to $439 million.

cases.question: Which products drove Eli Lilly's revenue growth in 2024, and what offset it?
cases.expected_text: Lilly's 2024 revenue increase came mainly from higher volume and, to a lesser extent, higher realized prices, led by Mounjaro, Zepbound and Verzenio. Trulicity partially offset the growth: its U.S. revenue fell 32% on lower volume due to competitive dynamics and supply constraints in the first half of 2024, and outside the U.S. it fell 8% due to competitive dynamics and demand-management actions.
key_points: Growth came mainly from volume and, to a lesser extent, higher realized prices.
Mounjaro, Zepbound and Verzenio were the main drivers.
Trulicity declines (competition and supply constraints) partially offset the growth.

passages.quote: Revenue increased in 2024 driven by increased volume and, to a lesser extent, higher realized prices. The increase in revenue in 2024 was primarily driven by Mounjaro, Zepbound, and Verzenio, partially offset by Trulicity.

Revenue of Trulicity decreased 32 percent in the U.S., driven by decreased volume primarily due to competitive dynamics and supply constraints during the first half of 2024. Revenue outside the U.S. decreased 8 percent, driven by decreased volume primarily due to competitive dynamics and actions we have taken to manage demand.

cases.question: Why does Lockheed Martin consider fixed-price development contracts risky, and how does it account for an expected loss on a contract (2023 10-K)?
cases.expected_text: Lockheed Martin says fixed-price development work or fixed-price production options, especially on competitively bid programs, is inherently riskier than cost-reimbursable work because revenue is fixed while the estimated costs to complete development programs are subject to significant variability. The technical complexity of such programs combined with a fixed-price structure raises the risk that costs exceed expectations, resulting in reduced margins, operating profit or reach-forward losses. When estimated total contract costs exceed the estimated transaction price, it records a provision for the entire loss at the contract level in the period the loss becomes evident, which it calls a reach-forward loss.
key_points: Fixed-price development is riskier because revenue is fixed while costs to complete are highly uncertain.
Technical complexity under a fixed price can lead to reduced margins, operating profit or reach-forward losses.
A reach-forward loss is recorded in full, at the contract level, in the period the loss becomes evident.

passages.quote: Fixed-price development work or fixed-price production options, especially on competitively bid programs, is inherently riskier than cost-reimbursable work because the revenue is fixed, while the estimates of costs required to complete these contracts are subject to significant variability due to the nature of development programs.

The technical complexity coupled with the fixed-price contract structure of certain of our ongoing development programs or new programs increases the risk that our costs will be greater than anticipated, resulting in reduced margins, operating profit, or reach-forward losses during the period of contract performance or upon contract award, all of which could be significant to our operating results, cash flows, or financial condition.

When estimates of total costs to be incurred on a contract exceed total estimates of the transaction price, a provision for the entire loss is determined at the contract level and is recorded in the period in which the loss is evident, which we refer to as a reach-forward loss.

cases.question: Why does McDonald's emphasize franchising, and how much of its system was franchised at the end of 2025?
cases.expected_text: About 95% of McDonald's 45,356 restaurants were franchised at year-end 2025. McDonald's says it is primarily a franchisor and believes franchising is paramount to delivering great-tasting food, locally relevant customer experiences and driving profitability: franchising lets an individual be their own employer and control employment, marketing and pricing decisions while benefiting from McDonald's global brand, operating system and financial resources.
key_points: About 95% of 45,356 restaurants were franchised at year-end 2025.
Franchising is seen as paramount to great food, locally relevant experiences and profitability.
Franchisees control employment, marketing and pricing while using the brand and system.

passages.quote: Of the 45,356 McDonald's restaurants at year-end 2025, approximately 95% were franchised.

The Company is primarily a franchisor and believes franchising is paramount to delivering great-tasting food, locally relevant customer experiences and driving profitability. Franchising enables an individual to be their own employer and maintain control over all employment related matters, marketing and pricing decisions, while also benefiting from the strength of McDonald’s global brand, operating system and financial resources.

cases.question: What does Meta's 2024 10-K say about Reality Labs' losses and its outlook for them?
cases.expected_text: Meta says its significant investments in Reality Labs have generated only limited revenue and reduced its operating margin and profitability, and it expects the adverse impact to continue for the foreseeable future. Reality Labs reduced 2024 operating profit by about $17.73 billion; its loss from operations rose $1.61 billion (10%) from 2023, mainly because of higher employee compensation and infrastructure costs. Meta expects Reality Labs investments and operating losses to increase in 2025.
key_points: Reality Labs has generated limited revenue and reduces Meta's operating margin and profitability.
Reality Labs reduced 2024 operating profit by about $17.73 billion.
The RL operating loss grew $1.61 billion (10%) in 2024, mainly on higher employee compensation and infrastructure costs.
Meta expects Reality Labs operating losses to increase in 2025.

passages.quote: Some of these investments, particularly our significant investments in Reality Labs, have generated only limited revenue and reduced our operating margin and profitability, and we expect the adverse financial impact of such investments to continue for the foreseeable future. For example, our investments in Reality Labs reduced our 2024 overall operating profit by approximately $17.73 billion, and we expect our Reality Labs investments and operating losses to increase in 2025.

RL loss from operations in 2024 increased $1.61 billion, or 10%, compared to 2023, driven by an increase in RL costs and expenses. RL costs and expenses increased primarily due to increases in employee compensation and infrastructure costs.

cases.question: What risks does Merck's 2025 10-K identify around its dependence on Keytruda?
cases.expected_text: Keytruda represented 49% of Merck's total sales in 2025, so events affecting it could significantly hurt results. Merck expects Keytruda sales to be materially hurt by biosimilar competition between 2028 and 2029; two further patents in the compound patent family run to 2029 through patent term adjustment, but Merck expects them to be litigated. Merck also expects Keytruda to be selected in 2027 for government price setting, effective January 1, 2029, after which it expects U.S. Keytruda sales to decline materially.
key_points: Keytruda was 49% of Merck's total 2025 sales.
Merck expects biosimilar competition to materially hurt Keytruda sales between 2028 and 2029.
Merck expects government price setting for Keytruda effective January 1, 2029, and a material decline in U.S. sales after that.

passages.quote: In particular, in the aggregate, in 2025, sales of Keytruda represented 49% of the Company’s total sales.
Also, the Company expects that sales of Keytruda will be materially negatively impacted by biosimilar competition between 2028 and 2029.

The compound patent family contains two additional patents that expire in 2029 due to patent term adjustment resulting from patent office delay. These patents are based on the initial discovery of the active ingredient in Keytruda. While these patents may provide additional protection, the Company expects that they will be the subject of litigation in the future.

Furthermore, the Company expects that Keytruda will be selected in 2027 for government price setting, which would become effective on January 1, 2029, and the Company expects that, as a result, U.S. sales of Keytruda will decline materially after that time.

cases.question: How does Microsoft describe its partnership with OpenAI in its fiscal 2023 10-K?
cases.expected_text: Microsoft describes a long-term partnership with OpenAI, which it calls a leading AI research and deployment company. Microsoft deploys OpenAI's models across its consumer and enterprise products; Azure is OpenAI's exclusive cloud provider and powers all of OpenAI's workloads; and Microsoft has increased investment in specialized supercomputing systems to accelerate OpenAI's research.
key_points: Microsoft deploys OpenAI's models across its consumer and enterprise products.
Azure is OpenAI's exclusive cloud provider and powers all its workloads.
Microsoft has increased investment in supercomputing systems to accelerate OpenAI's research.

passages.quote: We have a long-term partnership with OpenAI, a leading AI research and deployment company. We deploy OpenAI’s models across our consumer and enterprise products. As OpenAI’s exclusive cloud provider, Azure powers all of OpenAI's workloads. We have also increased our investments in the development and deployment of specialized supercomputing systems to accelerate OpenAI’s research.

cases.question: What change in accounting estimate did Microsoft make for its server and network equipment in fiscal 2023, why, and what was its effect?
cases.expected_text: Microsoft extended the estimated useful lives of its server and network equipment from four to six years, citing investments in software that made operating that equipment more efficient, and advances in technology. The change in accounting estimate took effect beginning in fiscal 2023 and increased fiscal 2023 operating income by $3.7 billion and net income by $3.0 billion ($0.40 per share); depreciation expense declined in fiscal 2023 as a result.
key_points: Useful lives of server and network equipment were extended from four to six years.
The reason was software-driven efficiency gains and advances in technology.
The change raised fiscal 2023 operating income by $3.7 billion and net income by $3.0 billion.

passages.quote: Due to investments in software that increased efficiencies in how we operate our server and network equipment, as well as advances in technology, we determined we should increase the estimated useful lives of both server and network equipment from four years to six years. This change in accounting estimate was effective beginning fiscal year 2023. Based on the carrying amount of server and network equipment included in property and equipment, net as of June 30, 2022, the effect of this change in estimate for fiscal year 2023 was an increase in operating income of $3.7 billion and net income of $3.0 billion, or $0.40 per both basic and diluted share.
Depreciation expense declined in fiscal year 2023 due to the change in estimated useful lives of our server and network equipment.

cases.question: What did Micron's fiscal 2023 10-K say about competitive pressure from China, including the Cyberspace Administration of China decision?
cases.expected_text: Micron says it faces increasing competition because the Chinese government and state-affiliated entities are investing heavily in semiconductor companies such as YMTC and CXMT. In addition, the CAC decided on May 21, 2023 that critical information infrastructure operators in China may not purchase Micron products, which affected Micron's ability to compete effectively in China and elsewhere.
key_points: Chinese government-backed investment in competitors such as YMTC and CXMT increases competition.
On May 21, 2023 the CAC barred critical information infrastructure operators in China from buying Micron products.
The decision hurt Micron's ability to compete in China and elsewhere.

passages.quote: In particular, we face the threat of increasing competition as a result of significant investment in the semiconductor industry by the Chinese government and various state-owned or affiliated entities, in companies such as Yangtze Memory Technologies Co., Ltd. (“YMTC”) and ChangXin Memory Technologies, Inc. (“CXMT”). In addition, the May 21, 2023 decision by China’s Cyberspace Administration (the “CAC”) that critical information infrastructure operators in China may not purchase Micron products had an impact on our ability to compete effectively in China and elsewhere.

cases.question: How does Netflix amortize its content assets, per its 2023 10-K?
cases.expected_text: Netflix amortizes licensed and produced content in cost of revenues, based on historical and estimated viewing patterns, over the shorter of each title's contractual window, its estimated period of use, or ten years, starting in the month of first availability. Amortization is accelerated because more viewing is expected up front, and film amortization is more accelerated than TV series. On average over 90% of a licensed or produced content asset is expected to be amortized within four years after first availability.
key_points: Content is amortized based on historical and estimated viewing patterns, over the shorter of the window, estimated use, or ten years.
Amortization is on an accelerated basis, more so for film than TV series.
Over 90% of an asset is expected to be amortized within four years.

passages.quote: Based on factors including historical and estimated viewing patterns, we amortize the content assets (licensed and produced) in “Cost of revenues” on the Consolidated Statements of Operations over the shorter of each title's contractual window of availability or estimated period of use or ten years, beginning with the month of first availability. The amortization is on an accelerated basis, as we typically expect more upfront viewing, and film amortization is more accelerated than TV series amortization.
On average, over 90% of a licensed or produced content asset is expected to be amortized within four years

cases.question: What explained the change in Netflix's streaming revenues in 2023?
cases.expected_text: Streaming revenues rose 7% in 2023, mainly because average paying memberships grew 8%, partly offset by a 1% decline in average monthly revenue per paying membership. The ARM decline reflected changes in plan mix and faster membership growth in lower-ARM regions, partly offset by limited price increases; unfavorable foreign exchange movements also weighed on revenues.
key_points: Growth in average paying memberships (8%) drove the increase.
Average monthly revenue per paying membership fell 1% because of plan mix and growth in lower-revenue regions.
Unfavorable foreign exchange rates also reduced streaming revenues.

passages.quote: Streaming revenues for the year ended December 31, 2023 increased 7% as compared to the year ended December 31, 2022, primarily due to the 8% growth in average paying memberships, partially offset by a 1% decrease in average monthly revenue per paying membership. The decrease in average monthly revenue per paying membership was primarily due to changes in plan mix, higher membership growth in regions with lower average monthly revenue per paying membership, partially offset by limited price increases. Additionally, streaming revenues for the year ended December 31, 2023 were further impacted by unfavorable fluctuations in foreign exchange rates.

cases.question: What drove NVIDIA's Data Center revenue growth and gross margin change in fiscal 2025?
cases.expected_text: Data Center revenue rose 142% in fiscal 2025, driven by demand for the Hopper accelerated computing platform used for large language models, recommendation engines and generative AI applications; NVIDIA began shipping production Blackwell systems in the fourth quarter. Gross margin rose to 75.0% from 72.7%, primarily because of a higher mix of Data Center revenue.
key_points: Data Center growth was driven by demand for the Hopper platform for LLMs, recommendation engines and generative AI.
Production Blackwell systems began shipping in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025.
Gross margin increased mainly because of a higher mix of Data Center revenue.

passages.quote: Data Center revenue for fiscal year 2025 was up 142% from a year ago. The strong year-on-year growth was driven by demand for our Hopper architecture accelerated computing platform used for large language models, recommendation engines, and generative AI applications. We began shipping production systems of the Blackwell architecture in the fourth quarter of fiscal year 2025.
Gross margins increased to 75.0% in fiscal year 2025 from 72.7% in fiscal year 2024. The year over year increase was primarily driven by a higher mix of Data Center revenue.

cases.question: How have U.S. export controls affected NVIDIA's business according to its fiscal 2025 10-K?
cases.expected_text: NVIDIA says that over the past three years it has been subject to a series of shifting and expanding U.S. export control restrictions that affect its ability to serve customers outside the United States, and it had not received licenses to ship the restricted products to China. If the rules change further, it may be unable to sell its inventory of such products or to develop replacement products that are not subject to the licensing requirements, effectively excluding it from all or part of the China market and other affected markets, including the Middle East and countries designated 'Tier 2' by the AI Diffusion IFR. Its Data Center revenue in China grew in fiscal 2025 but, as a share of total Data Center revenue, remains well below the levels seen before export controls began in October 2023.
key_points: Over the past three years NVIDIA has faced a series of shifting and expanding U.S. export restrictions that affect its ability to serve customers outside the U.S.
NVIDIA had not received licenses to ship the restricted products to China.
Further changes could leave inventory unsellable and exclude it from all or part of China, the Middle East and AI Diffusion 'Tier 2' countries.
China Data Center revenue grew in fiscal 2025 but remains well below pre-control levels as a share of Data Center revenue.

passages.quote: Over the past three years, we have been subject to a series of shifting and expanding export control restrictions, impacting our ability to serve customers outside the United States.
To date, we have not received licenses to ship these restricted products to China.

In the event of such change, we may be unable to sell our inventory of such products and may be unable to develop replacement products not subject to the licensing requirements, effectively excluding us from all or part of the China market, as well as other impacted markets, including the Middle East and countries designated “Tier 2” by the AI Diffusion IFR.
Our Data Center revenue in China grew in fiscal year 2025. As a percentage of total Data Center revenue, it remains well below levels seen prior to the onset of export controls in October 2023.

cases.question: What does Oracle's fiscal 2024 10-K say about the risks and expected costs of expanding its data center capacity for Oracle Cloud?
cases.expected_text: If Oracle cannot secure data center capacity at affordable rates or does not accurately plan its infrastructure capacity, its profitability may decline. It has entered, and expects to keep entering, long-term operating leases with third-party data center providers that generally require significant fees to exit early. Data centers in the geographies it relies on may be unavailable on commercially reasonable terms or at all, and Oracle does not control the operation of these third-party data centers, which may suffer service interruptions from events beyond its control. Oracle expects its cloud services and license support expenses to keep growing in fiscal 2025 as it increases data center capacity and establishes data centers in new geographic locations.
key_points: Inability to secure affordable data center capacity or poor capacity planning could reduce profitability.
Long-term leases with third-party data center providers carry significant early-termination fees.
Capacity may be unavailable on reasonable terms, and Oracle does not control third-party data centers, which may suffer interruptions.
Oracle expects cloud services and license support expenses to keep growing in fiscal 2025 as it adds capacity.

passages.quote: If we are unable to secure data center capacity at affordable rates or do not accurately plan for our infrastructure capacity requirements, our profitability may decline.

In connection with these investments, we entered, and expect to continue to enter, into long-term operating lease commitments with third-party data center providers that generally require us to pay significant contract termination fees to early exit such obligations should our strategies change, which could adversely impact our profitability and cash flows.
Data centers in geographies that we rely on may also be unavailable on commercially reasonable terms or at all.

Moreover, we do not control the operation of these third-party data centers, and they may suffer interruptions in service from events beyond our control, including from acts of government, natural events, power loss, break-ins or misconduct by those third parties.

Our cloud services and license support expenses have grown in recent periods, and we expect this trend to continue during fiscal 2025 as we increase our existing data center capacity and establish data centers in new geographic locations in order to meet current and expected customer demand.

cases.question: What restructuring did Procter & Gamble announce in fiscal 2025 and what costs and headcount impact does it expect?
cases.expected_text: In June 2025 P&G announced a portfolio and productivity plan to streamline its portfolio and organization and improve its cost structure and competitiveness. It expects about $1.5 to $2.0 billion of before-tax restructuring costs over two years (including this plan and the ongoing one), with half of this plan's costs incurred by the end of fiscal 2026 and the rest in fiscal 2027. The restructuring includes a reduction of up to 7,000 non-manufacturing overhead positions by the end of fiscal 2027.
key_points: In June 2025 P&G announced a plan to streamline its portfolio and organization and improve costs and competitiveness.
It expects $1.5-$2.0 billion of before-tax restructuring costs over two years, half by the end of fiscal 2026.
It plans to cut up to 7,000 non-manufacturing overhead positions by the end of fiscal 2027.

passages.quote: In June 2025, the Company announced a portfolio and productivity plan to streamline its portfolio and organization to improve its cost structure and competitiveness. The Company expects to incur approximately $1.5 to $2.0 billion in before-tax restructuring costs over a two-year period, including costs incurred as part of this plan and the ongoing plan. The Company expects to incur half of the costs under this plan by the end of fiscal 2026, with the remainder incurred in fiscal 2027.
These restructuring activities include a plan for a reduction of up to 7,000 non-manufacturing overhead personnel by the end of fiscal 2027.

cases.question: What customer-concentration and vertical-integration risks does Qualcomm describe in its fiscal 2024 10-K, particularly regarding Apple?
cases.expected_text: Revenues from Apple, Samsung and Xiaomi each made up 10% or more of Qualcomm's fiscal 2024 consolidated revenues. Apple acquired Intel's modem assets in December 2019 and is developing its own modem products with them, so Qualcomm expects Apple to use its own modems rather than Qualcomm's in some or all of its future devices. Qualcomm also notes that certain of its customers in China have developed, and others may develop, their own integrated circuit products and use them in their devices instead of Qualcomm's.
key_points: A few customers (Apple, Samsung, Xiaomi) each account for 10% or more of revenues.
Qualcomm expects Apple to use its own modem products instead of Qualcomm's in some or all future devices.
Chinese OEMs are also developing in-house chips, a further vertical-integration risk.

passages.quote: In fiscal 2024, revenues from Apple, Samsung and Xiaomi each comprised 10% or more of our consolidated revenues.

In December 2019, Apple acquired Intel’s modem assets and is developing its own modem products using those assets. Accordingly, we expect Apple to use its own modem products, rather than our products, in some or all of its future devices.

Certain of our customers in China have developed, and others may in the future develop, their own integrated circuit products and use such integrated circuit products in their devices rather than our integrated circuit products

cases.question: What key-person risk does Tesla describe regarding Elon Musk in its 2022 10-K?
cases.expected_text: Tesla says it is highly dependent on the services of Elon Musk, Technoking of Tesla and its Chief Executive Officer. Although he spends significant time with Tesla and is highly active in management, he does not devote his full time and attention to Tesla: he is also CEO and CTO of SpaceX, CEO of Twitter, and involved in other emerging technology ventures. Tesla also flags that if Musk were forced to sell shares he has pledged to secure personal loans, such sales could cause its stock price to decline.
key_points: Tesla is highly dependent on the services of Elon Musk.
Musk does not devote his full time to Tesla because he also leads SpaceX and Twitter and other ventures.
Forced sales of shares Musk pledged for personal loans could depress the stock price.

passages.quote: We are highly dependent on the services of Elon Musk, Technoking of Tesla and our Chief Executive Officer.

Although Mr. Musk spends significant time with Tesla and is highly active in our management, he does not devote his full time and attention to Tesla. Mr. Musk also currently serves as Chief Executive Officer and Chief Technical Officer of Space Exploration Technologies Corp., a developer and manufacturer of space launch vehicles, Chief Executive Officer of Twitter, Inc., a social media company, and is involved in other emerging technology ventures.

If Elon Musk were forced to sell shares of our common stock, either that he has pledged to secure certain personal loan obligations, or in satisfaction of other obligations, such sales could cause our stock price to decline.

cases.question: What are Tesla's automotive regulatory credits and how are they recognized (2022 10-K)?
cases.expected_text: Tesla earns tradable credits under regulations on zero-emission vehicles, greenhouse gas, fuel economy and clean fuel, and sells them to other regulated entities who use them to meet emission standards. Sales are recognized in automotive regulatory credits revenue. This revenue is tied to Tesla's new vehicle production, sales and negotiated pricing; Tesla monetizes credits proactively as new vehicles are sold under standing arrangements with buyers, typically close to production and delivery or to regulatory changes affecting the credits.
key_points: Tesla earns tradable credits under ZEV, greenhouse gas, fuel economy and clean fuel regulations and sells them to other regulated entities.
Sales are recognized as automotive regulatory credits revenue.
Credits are monetized as vehicles are sold under standing arrangements, so the revenue follows vehicle production and sales.

passages.quote: We earn tradable credits in the operation of our business under various regulations related to zero-emission vehicles (“ZEVs”), greenhouse gas, fuel economy and clean fuel. We sell these credits to other regulated entities who can use the credits to comply with emission standards and other regulatory requirements. Sales of these credits are recognized within automotive regulatory credits revenue in our consolidated financial statements included elsewhere in this Annual Report on Form 10-K.

Our revenue from automotive regulatory credits is directly related to our new vehicle production, sales and pricing negotiated with our customers. We monetize them proactively as new vehicles are sold based on standing arrangements with buyers of such credits, typically as close as possible to the production and delivery of the vehicle or changes in regulation impacting the credits.

cases.question: What does TSMC's 2024 annual report say about its Arizona expansion and U.S. CHIPS Act support?
cases.expected_text: Construction of TSMC Arizona's first fab began in April 2021 and volume production started by the end of 2024; a second fab, announced in December 2022, is under construction, and a third was announced in April 2024. The U.S. Department of Commerce agreed to award TSMC Arizona up to US$6.6 billion in direct funding for its Phoenix fabs, and TSMC Arizona can draw down up to US$5 billion in government loans; TSMC gives an irrevocable, unconditional guarantee of TSMC Arizona's financial obligations to the Department of Commerce. In March 2025 TSMC announced plans for three more U.S. fabs, two advanced packaging facilities and an R&D center.
key_points: The first Arizona fab reached volume production by the end of 2024; a second is under construction and a third was announced.
CHIPS Act support: up to US$6.6 billion direct funding and up to US$5 billion in loans, with TSMC guaranteeing TSMC Arizona's obligations.
In March 2025 TSMC announced three more U.S. fabs, two advanced packaging facilities and an R&D center.

passages.quote: Construction on the first facility commenced in April 2021 and volume production commenced by the end of 2024. In December 2022, we announced a plan for TSMC Arizona to build and operate a second semiconductor manufacturing facility, which is currently under construction. In April 2024, we further announced a plan for TSMC Arizona to build and operate a third semiconductor manufacturing facility.

Under this agreement, the DOC agrees to award TSMC Arizona up to US$6.6 billion in direct funding related to TSMC Arizona’s semiconductor manufacturing facilities in Phoenix, Arizona (the “Projects”).

In addition to the Direct Funding Agreement, TSMC Arizona also entered into a loan guarantee agreement and several ancillary agreements with the DOC (the “Loan Agreements”), under which TSMC Arizona is entitled to draw down up to US$5 billion in government loans for the Projects.

In connection with the Direct Funding Agreement and the Loan Agreements, the Company entered into certain guarantee agreements, under which the Company agrees to provide an irrevocable, absolute and unconditional guarantee to the DOC regarding any financial obligations owed by TSMC Arizona to the DOC.
In March 2025, we further announced our intention to build three additional semiconductor manufacturing facilities, two advanced packaging facilities and a R&D center in the United States.

cases.question: How does Texas Instruments describe its capital allocation approach and its outlook for capital expenditures in its 2023 10-K?
cases.expected_text: Disciplined allocation of capital is the second element of TI's strategy to maximize free cash flow per share growth; it spans how TI selects R&D projects, develops new capabilities, invests in manufacturing capacity, approaches acquisitions and returns cash to its owners. From 2014 to 2023 it allocated $94 billion, the largest share to organic growth (R&D, sales and marketing, capital expenditures and working capital for inventory). It expects capital expenditures to stay higher than historical levels as it invests in manufacturing and technology as part of long-term capacity planning. The U.S. CHIPS and Science Act of August 2022 established a 25% investment tax credit for certain U.S. semiconductor manufacturing investments; TI expects to receive the cash benefit of that credit for qualifying capital expenditures and has applied for the Act's manufacturing grants.
key_points: Disciplined capital allocation is the second element of TI's strategy to maximize free cash flow per share growth.
Of $94 billion allocated over 2014-2023, the largest share went to organic growth; allocation also covers acquisitions and returning cash to owners.
Capex is expected to stay higher than historical levels to build manufacturing capacity.
TI expects the CHIPS Act's 25% investment tax credit on qualifying capex and has applied for manufacturing grants.

passages.quote: The second element of our strategy to maximize free cash flow per share growth is disciplined allocation of capital.
This spans how we select R&D projects, develop new capabilities like TI.com, invest in new manufacturing capacity or how we think about acquisitions and returning cash to our owners.
Over a 10-year period from 2014 to 2023, we allocated $94 billion, which reinforces the importance of discipline in capital allocation.
The largest allocation over this period was to drive organic growth, which includes investments in R&D, sales and marketing, capital expenditures and working capital for inventory.

As we continue to invest to strengthen our competitive advantage in manufacturing and technology as part of our long-term capacity planning, our capital expenditures are expected to continue to be higher than historical levels.

In August 2022, the U.S. government enacted the U.S. CHIPS and Science Act, which provides funding for manufacturing grants and research investments and establishes a 25% investment tax credit for certain investments in U.S. semiconductor manufacturing.

We expect to receive the cash benefit associated with the investment tax credit for qualifying capital expenditures in future periods, and we have submitted applications for the manufacturing grants provided by the legislation.

cases.question: How did Union Pacific use its operating cash in 2024, and what capital plan does it describe for 2025?
cases.expected_text: In 2024 Union Pacific generated $9.3 billion of operating cash, paid down $1.3 billion of long-term debt, paid $3.2 billion in dividends and repurchased $1.5 billion of shares. For 2025 it expects a capital plan of about $3.4 billion, consistent with 2024, to support its growth strategy, improve the safety, resiliency and operational efficiency of the network, harden its infrastructure and replace older assets, including modernizing its locomotive fleet and acquiring freight cars for replacement and growth.
key_points: 2024 operating cash funded debt paydown, dividends and share repurchases.
The 2025 capital plan is about $3.4 billion, consistent with 2024.
Capital goes to growth, network safety, resiliency and efficiency, infrastructure hardening and replacing older assets (locomotives, freight cars).

passages.quote: During 2024, we generated $9.3 billion of cash provided by operating activities, paid down $1.3 billion of long-term debt, paid $3.2 billion in dividends, and repurchased shares totaling $1.5 billion.

Capital Plan – In 2025, we expect our capital plan to be approximately $3.4 billion, consistent with 2024. We plan to continue to make investments to support our growth strategy, improve the safety, resiliency, and operational efficiency of the network, harden our infrastructure, and replace older assets, including modernization of our locomotive fleet and acquiring freight cars to support replacement and growth opportunities.

cases.question: What does UPS's 2024 10-K say about its agreement with Amazon and the network changes it plans in response?
cases.expected_text: Amazon accounted for 11.8% of UPS's 2024 consolidated revenues. In the first quarter of 2025 UPS reached an agreement in principle with Amazon that will reduce Amazon's volume by more than 50% by June 2026, and UPS is making business and operational changes to match its workforce to its activity and eliminate stranded costs; if it cannot reduce costs, its profitability could be materially impacted. A U.S. network reconfiguration, an expansion of its Network of the Future program, could close up to 10% of its buildings in 2025 and shrink its vehicle and aircraft fleets and workforce; UPS cannot yet estimate the total cost. It expects to partly offset those costs through Efficiency Reimagined initiatives, an end-to-end process redesign expected to yield about $1.0 billion in annualized savings starting in 2025.
key_points: Amazon was 11.8% of UPS's 2024 consolidated revenues.
Under an agreement in principle, Amazon's volume will fall by more than 50% by June 2026.
UPS is matching its workforce to activity and eliminating stranded costs; failure to cut costs could materially hurt profitability.
A U.S. network reconfiguration may close up to 10% of buildings in 2025, and its total cost cannot yet be estimated.
Efficiency Reimagined is expected to save about $1.0 billion a year, starting in 2025, partly offsetting the reconfiguration costs.

passages.quote: For the year ended December 31, 2024, one customer, Amazon.com, Inc. and its affiliates, accounted for 11.8% of our consolidated revenues. In the first quarter of 2025, we entered into an agreement in principle with this customer that will provide for a reduction in their volume by more than 50% by June 2026.
In connection therewith, we are making certain business and operational changes intended to match our workforce to our activity and eliminate our stranded costs.
In the event we are not able to successfully reduce our costs in connection therewith, our profitability could be materially impacted.

This network reconfiguration, which is an expansion of our Network of the Future program, is expected to result in exit activities that could result in the closure of up to 10% of our buildings in 2025, a reduction in the size of our vehicle and aircraft fleets, and a decrease in the size of our workforce, which we expect will lead to additional expense.

We are not yet able to determine the specific assets or extent of our workforce that will be impacted by this network reconfiguration, the timing of those changes or any associated charges and expenses and therefore are not currently able to provide an estimate of the total cost or the cost by period.
We expect to partially offset the anticipated costs associated with this network reconfiguration through our Efficiency Reimagined initiatives.
Efficiency Reimagined initiatives are an end-to-end process redesign being undertaken to align our organizational processes to the network reconfiguration.
These initiatives are expected to yield approximately $1.0 billion in annualized savings, which we expect to begin realizing during 2025.

cases.question: What drove the changes in Walmart's gross profit rate and operating expense rate in fiscal 2025?
cases.expected_text: Walmart's gross profit rate rose 40 basis points in fiscal 2025, mainly from the Walmart U.S. segment managing prices in line with its competitive price gaps and from growth in higher-margin businesses globally, partly offset by a mix shift into lower-margin merchandise categories. Operating expenses as a percentage of net sales rose 36 basis points, mainly from higher variable pay after exceeding planned performance, more marketing and higher depreciation.
key_points: Gross profit rate improved because of Walmart U.S. price management and growth in higher-margin businesses.
A mix shift into lower-margin merchandise partly offset the gross margin gain.
The operating expense rate rose because of higher variable pay, marketing and depreciation.

passages.quote: Our gross profit rate increased 40 and 27 basis points for fiscal 2025 and 2024, respectively, when compared to the previous fiscal year.

The increases were primarily driven by the Walmart U.S. segment, due to managing prices aligned to our competitive historic price gaps, as well as growth in higher margin businesses globally, partially offset by mix shifts into lower margin merchandise categories.
Our operating expenses as a percentage of net sales increased 36 and decreased 60 basis points for fiscal 2025 and 2024, respectively, when compared to the previous fiscal year.
The increase for fiscal 2025 was primarily due to higher variable pay as a result of exceeding planned performance, increased marketing and higher depreciation expenses.
